items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

A marriage ca. 1838-1845 would most likely be in Ireland (church registers), or in Pennsylvania if they emigrated first. It confirms the couple as a unit, supplies a mother's name (a maiden name only if this was her first marriage), and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates the father named only by census co-residence. It then follows him through the 1860, 1870 (the Ancestry search you asked for) and 1880 censuses to see who lived with him. Next come church records of his death or burial, his marriage and his children's baptisms. After those it looks for the marriage of his probable father, Thomas Flynn, and for Thomas's will or estate papers. Naturalization papers and records of possible siblings and neighbors come last. They may show where in Ireland the family came from.

Next, the FamilySearch items will be searched in order, and the Ancestry 1870 census search will be prepared for you to run.

Per loc_001 statewide registration began 1906, so a 1908 certificate exists and its informant/parents fields may name father and mother (maiden name), a derivative record to be tested against later evidence. Read the image, not just the index.

Timeline t_001 flags a gap 1851-1860 and the 1860 census as not yet searched. The tree already holds the 1850 household (dwelling 84, Thomas Flynn, Patrick age 5, F1 birth ~1845 Ireland); 1850 does not state relationships, so 1860 tests whether Patrick still sits in Thomas's household and names the other members, including a possible mother.

Bridges 1860 to 1880 and shows whether Patrick, now about 25, is in his own household or still with Thomas, and who else lives there. Search Flynn with variants (Flinn, Flin, O'Flynn) and ages 22-28, birthplace Ireland, since tree F1 gives Ireland while the objective says Pennsylvania; that conflict is itself to be tested.

The 1880 schedule records each person's relationship to the head and parents' birthplaces, which 1850-1870 do not. It can show Thomas or a widowed mother in or near Patrick's household and gives the parents' birthplaces as a check on Ireland.

items.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Roman Catholic parishes, Archdiocese of Philadelphia)
items.rationale: Patrick's own death/burial entry. Tree F1 places birth in Ireland ca. 1845, so a Pennsylvania baptism does not exist and an Irish baptism is out of reach until the origin is known; a burial or sacramental death entry and cemetery record near 1908-03-12 can state age, birthplace or parents. loc_001: registers are held by the parish/diocese, not the county, and some coal-region church films are browse-only image groups, so plan an image browse where the index is empty.

Patrick's own marriage record and baptisms of his children (sponsors, spouse's family, possible grandparent names). No marriage is yet in the tree; the entry may give birthplace or parents, and the date fixes when he left his father's household. Catholic registers sit at parish level per loc_001.

items.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, and Ireland (county of origin unknown)
items.rationale: Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (tree I2, b. ~1818 Ireland) to the unknown mother of Patrick; no wife is in the tree, so no surname is assumed. A marriage ca. 1838-1845 would most likely be in Ireland (church registers), or in Pennsylvania if they emigrated first. It confirms the couple as a unit, supplies a mother's name (a maiden name only if this was her first marriage), and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates the father named only by census co-residence. Thomas Flynn was born ca. 1818, so his death could fall anywhere from 1850 to about 1900; window sized to his lifespan, not Patrick's. loc_001: the Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811, a primary source naming heirs. A will or administration naming Patrick as son is direct evidence; it also names the mother and siblings.

Naturalization records for Thomas and Patrick Flynn may state birthplace and arrival date, naming the Irish origin. loc_001 notes coal-region naturalization films can be browse-only image groups, so expect an image browse by volume rather than a name search.

FAN item: the neighbors on the 1850 page near dwelling 84 and any Flynn siblings. Baptisms, marriages and burials of siblings, and sponsors, can name the same parents, and neighbors from the same Irish area suggest the origin parish. Reveals Patrick's parentage through siblings' records.

items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

sources.title: Rowan County, North Carolina Marriage Records
sources.author: Rowan County Clerk

entry.rationale: Target record of the question. loc_001 lists North Carolina, Rowan County Probate Records, 1753-1970 and says the probate index is full-text searchable but only partly name-indexed, so run a keyword search on Voss (and variants Vos, Voss, Foss, Faust-style misspellings) across the whole window rather than browsing by year. Window is sized to the FATHER's plausible lifespan (death from Caroline's infancy in 1839 to about 1899), not her 1858 marriage. Look for wills, estate inventories, administrations and divisions naming a daughter Caroline, possibly under a married name.

Tree fact F2 records Caroline's marriage ~1858 in Rowan County, sourced from Rowan County Marriage Records (S1). Re-read that entry and the marriage bond: the bondsman or witness is often the bride's father or brother (FAN), and it gives the husband's name needed to find Caroline under her married name in probate heirs lists. Does not by itself prove parentage.

Find a Voss household in Rowan County with a daughter Caroline about age 11 (1850) to name a candidate father and siblings, and neighbors (FAN) who may be executors or appraisers. Candidate father is a lead only, not established. The 1860 census (collection returned by the national lookup, name-searchable) should show Caroline with her husband and nearby Voss households. Use it to build the surname list for the probate keyword search.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Caroline's candidate parents to each other, once a candidate father is named by items 1 and 3. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's maiden name (only if it was her first marriage; check for remarriage), and its date relative to 1839 corroborates the father. It does not by itself prove Caroline is their child.

Deeds from heirs and estate land divisions often name every child of a deceased landowner and their spouses, and boundary recitals name neighbors (FAN). Useful where the probate file is missing or unindexed (about 60% of the probate index is not name-indexed per loc_001). Window follows the father's lifespan.

County court minutes and orphan or guardianship records: if Caroline's father died while she was a minor (before about 1860), a guardian appointment or apprenticeship would name him. Complements item 1 for estates recorded in court minutes rather than probate files.

Caroline's own death, burial or obituary entry (no baptism or death record is in the tree). Gravestones, church burial registers and any post-1913 death certificate state age, birthplace and often parents' names; also reveals her married name and burial plot neighbors who may be Voss kin.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Catholic registers are held by the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia (loc_001). Also check cemetery records and obituary.

Patrick's own marriage(s), since the birth register may not exist. Marriage entries often name the home parish or parents. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 are name-searchable; also church marriage registers. Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 covers a later marriage. Each marriage should be found, as a later wife is not assumed to be the first.

The 1850 census (log_001, log_002) placed Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84; that is co-residence evidence only, with no relationship column in 1850. Trace the household in 1860 (S2 cited for the relationship), 1870 and 1880; the 1880 schedule states relationship to head and parents' birthplaces. Search Flynn spelling variants (Flinn, Flin, O'Flynn). Confirms the mother's identity and any remarriage.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

## Baiersbronn, Württemberg - 1800s

Church books are on Archion (parish page above).

entry.rationale: Katharina's own baptism entry names her parents directly. Tree holds only Birth 'about 1843, Baiersbronn, Württemberg' (no source), so the year is approximate: search 1840-1846. loc_001 says the Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn registers are on Archion (paid), not FamilySearch, and collections_search for Germany returned none, so this is an Archion browse by hand. Watch for variant spellings Seeger/Seger/Säger and Katharina/Catharina/Katarina.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (identified from the baptism in item 1): confirms the couple, supplies the mother's maiden name, and by date relative to c.1843 corroborates the pair. It does not alone prove Katharina is their child. If the mother had an earlier marriage, her maiden name may differ, so check for earlier marriages. Window set by parents' plausible ages (marriage c.1815-1845). Archion marriage register for Baiersbronn per loc_001.

Württemberg Familienregister (named in loc_001 as digitised on Archion) group parents and all children on one page with births, marriages and deaths. Locating the Seeger family page places Katharina with her parents and siblings, the record that links child to parents, and gives sibling and parent death dates.

Katharina's own marriage entry (probably also Baiersbronn, else wherever she lived) usually states her parents and her birth surname. Subject's own marriage is planned because the baptism may be hard to find: the birth year is only approximate and the birthplace (parish vs. hamlet) is unconfirmed. Archion marriage registers; start at Baiersbronn.

Katharina's own death or burial entry, dated from her birth through her likely lifespan, often gives age, birthplace and parents' names; the baptism may be unreachable because the birth year is approximate. Search the burial register where she last lived (start Baiersbronn); Archion.

FAN item: baptisms of Seeger siblings and their godparents (Taufpaten) and witnesses to Seeger marriages around Baiersbronn name the same parents and relatives, testing the parentage found in items 1-3 and covering the case where Katharina's own entry is missing. Window covers likely sibling births before and after 1843.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: FAN item. The tree records Thomas Flynn heading the 1850 household (dwelling 84, family 91) and the 1860 household (dwelling 112, family 119), with Patrick age 5 and 15, born Ireland. The relationship is only inferred from household position. Re-open those two pages and transcribe the 10-20 neighbouring households: surnames shared across both decades, Irish-born neighbours, and any Flynn/O'Flynn/Flinn household adjacent are candidate kin or fellow emigrants, and any other adults or children inside Thomas's own household (wife, siblings) that earlier extraction did not capture. Use variant spellings Flinn, Flin, Flyn, O'Flynn.

Ps_001 lists 1870, 1880 and 1900 as unsearched. 1880 is the first census stating relationship to head, so any Flynn household headed by Thomas, or Patrick's own household with a parent or in-law, would state it directly. 1900 gives Patrick's immigration year and neighbours. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found for Michael himself. No plan has yet been written for this question.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree and log: Michael was a farmer outside Schuylkill County in 1870 (log_001) and a miner in Schuylkill County in 1882 (log_002; tree F2, F3). The 1880 census is name-searchable (United States Census, 1880) and falls between those points; it shows whether he was already in the county, his occupation, household members (possibly Patrick, tree F4: Schuylkill resident 1875) and birthplaces of children, which date the move.

Tree source S2: Patrick Sheahan bought land from James Kelly, Deed Book 42 p. 118, 1875, so a brother-or-relative was in the county seven years before Michael, suggesting chain migration (the relationship of I1 and I2 is only via an unnamed shared parent I3 in the tree). Search Recorder of Deeds for Michael, Patrick and Kelly, and for leases, noting loc_001: laborers usually leased from mining companies, so absence of a Michael deed does not disprove mining work. FAN: Patrick and James Kelly.

Collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. Catholic registers (loc_001: Archdiocese of Philadelphia, held at parish) of baptisms of Michael's children, marriages and burials may give residence, origin parish and sponsors from Patrick's circle, dating arrival and showing kin ties. Searched under variants Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Shean, Shahan.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and records occupation, birthplace, years in the US and months unemployed; it tests whether mining work continued and corroborates the arrival date, and shows neighbours in the mining patch. Variant spellings as above.

Subject's own death entry: Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 are name-searchable (statewide registration began 1906 per loc_001). It states occupation, birthplace and parents, and may name years of residence; a death in a mining town with miner's lung or mining accident would corroborate lifelong mining. Also check Patrick's certificate for shared parent names.

Michael's own marriage: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages are name-searchable; entries give residence, occupation and sometimes parents, showing when and where he was working. Marriage may predate 1885 (this collection starts 1885), so also use church marriage entries from sequence 3.

Employment and context sources: colliery and coal company payrolls and employment books (e.g. Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, held in regional archives such as Hagley or county historical society; no tool has located specific holdings, so the researcher must identify them), mine inspector reports, and city directories 1880s. These are the only sources that could directly document recruitment or work, as opposed to inferring it from an occupation label. Also county histories describing 1880s labour demand and the strikes of the period.

Local newspapers (Pottsville, Shenandoah and similar) may report mining accidents, labour recruitment, arrivals or Sheahan family notices, giving context and possible motives other than work, such as family illness or following kin. Test against the alternatives to the family tradition.

Naturalization petitions: if Michael was an immigrant, loc_001 notes coal-region naturalization films may be browse-only (verify with volume_search at execution), so plan an image browse. Declarations give birthplace, arrival date and residence, which date the move and show whether he came directly to the coal region from Ireland or via another county.

Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill estate files, not a name search. Wills or estates of Michael, Patrick or the shared parent I3 could name kin, property and place of origin; window set by Michael and Patrick's likely lifespans into the 20th century, since a parent could die at any date.

This plan tests whether Michael Sheahan moved to Pennsylvania's coal country around 1882 to work in the mines, as the family story says. We know he was a farmer in 1870 and a miner in Schuylkill County by 1882, but nothing yet shows why he moved. The plan starts with the 1880 census to see where he was living and who was in his household. It then checks land records, because his possible brother Patrick bought land there in 1875, which suggests Michael followed family. After that it looks at church records, the 1900 census, and his marriage and death records. Mining company records, local newspapers, naturalization papers and wills come last, since they may be harder to reach.

Next, the FamilySearch records will be searched in that order, starting with the 1880 census.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

Records occupation, birthplace and household members (FAN).

loc_001: Catholic registers sit with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia parishes, not the county; the Schuylkill church collection is name-searchable. Baptisms of children, marriages, or transfers name residence and sometimes occupation and origin parish, dating arrival. Search Sheahan with variants Shehan, Sheehan, Shehan, Sheahen.

The 1880 and 1890 gap is bridged by 1900 (1890 schedules largely destroyed). Gives occupation, years in the US/immigration year, birthplace and neighbors in a mining patch; confirms continued mining work and mining-community neighbors who may be kin or fellow migrants.

Local coal-region papers (collieries hiring, strikes, accident and death notices naming miners) could name Michael's colliery or employer and arrival. Locate digitized papers via the Pennsylvania newspaper repositories; no tool result yet names a specific title, so find it on the repository's own site.

Employer and mine records: Pennsylvania mine inspectors' annual reports (list collieries and accident victims) and coal company payrolls/employment ledgers (held in regional archives) would document mining employment directly, the best test of the family tradition. Contextual and institutional; availability to be confirmed.

loc_001: coal-region naturalization films are browse-only (personCount 0 in volume results), so browse image-by-image after a volume_search. Declarations and petitions state birthplace, arrival date, residence and witnesses (FAN, often fellow miners) and may state occupation.

Window set by his plausible lifespan after 1882; also check children's marriages and death certificates, since the Pennsylvania county marriage series starts 1885.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.informant: Unknown household member reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The household member who provided the name is unknown. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have read a sign, heard a neighbor, or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

items.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn or wife)
items.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by a household member — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. Proximity is 'household_member' rather than 'unknown' because these facts could only come from someone in the household.

items.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)
items.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

items.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
items.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
items.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

items.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

items.informant: Ancestry transcriber (derivative of census enumerator)
items.informant_bias_notes: Derivative index — transcription errors possible

We know he was a child in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850, but the census doesn't say they were father and son. The plan starts with later censuses, his 1908 death certificate and his burial, since those may name his parents or his birthplace. After those it looks at records for possible brothers, sisters and neighbors, a full-text search of church pages, and naturalization papers. The 1850 census says he was born in Ireland, so some of the answers may lie in Irish records.

Next, the FamilySearch searches will run in that order, beginning with the 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Bridget (tree: b. ~1838 Ireland) bore about 9 children (1900 census, log_002), most likely in the Doyle marriage; Ellen's marriage record (log_003) names parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Baptisms name both parents and sponsors, the most direct way to enumerate children. Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; loc_001 notes Catholic registers stay with the Philadelphia diocese, so search Doyle with mother Halloran/Holloran/Halloren/Haloran and Doyle/Doil/Doyl variants, with no parish restriction since the parish is unknown.

United States Census 1860, 1870 and 1880 are name-searchable. The 1870 and 1880 schedules give relationship to head, so a John/Bridget Doyle household would list children by name and age; 1860 lists the household without relationships. Bridget remarried Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so 1880 may show Doyle children as stepchildren in the Kearney household. Search Doyle households with Bridget and Ellen, and Kearney 1880, with variant spellings.

The marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran has not been found; the Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 collections are name-searchable. It fixes the start of the union and so the birth window for children, and confirms this was Bridget's first marriage and John her first husband. The marriage may have occurred in Ireland or elsewhere, so a miss is informative. A marriage does not itself prove children.

John Doyle died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage (log_001), so an estate or administration file would name widow and heirs or minor children, and guardianship of minors may follow. Window is set by John's death (unknown, likely 1860s-1879) with allowance for later guardianship filings. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0); loc_001 says the Register of Wills holds records from 1811, so browse the Schuylkill volumes image by image, using volume_search to find them.

entry.repository: Find a Grave and parish cemetery records
entry.rationale: About 7 of 9 children died before 1900, many presumably as infants or children before 1906, when civil death registration began (loc_001), so church burial entries and gravestones are the main source for them. Look for John Doyle's burial and for Doyle children, often buried in a family plot. Children buried with Doyle or Kearney surnames may be found beside the parents.

John Doyle probably worked in the anthracite mines, so a mine accident or death notice could give his death date and surviving family. Search for his death and for children's death notices. Needed to date his death, which narrows the birth window of children.

FAN and sibling item. Ellen's marriage (log_003) names her parents; marriage records of other Doyle children (including the second surviving child, unidentified) in Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages name parents John Doyle and Bridget. Also review witnesses and sponsors on Ellen's marriage and baptism entries for siblings or relatives. Search Doyle marriages with parent names, plus Ellen's own children's baptisms for uncles and aunts as sponsors.

The 1900 Kearney household image (log_002) was read only for the fertility columns. Re-examine the whole household and neighbors for the second surviving child, then search the 1910 census (name-searchable) for Bridget and for Doyle adult children living nearby or as relatives. The window reaches 1910 because Bridget could still be living and the surviving children are then adults.

Bridget's own death (after 1900) falls within statewide registration (starts 1906, loc_001). Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable; search Bridget Kearney and Martin Kearney. The informant is often a child, which may name the surviving second child. Also Doyle children dying after 1906 with parents named.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Mikkel's birth (20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn); no parents or sources. The baptism entry names both parents and sponsors. Denmark, Church Books (2078555) is name-searchable but loc_001 says the Stagstrup register is only about 3% name-indexed, so browse the Stagstrup kirkebog images (1763-1814 volume) for Aug-Sep 1779, after a quick name search with variants (Mikkel/Michel/Mikkel, Nielsen/Nielsen/Nilsson, Blyeberg/Bly-berg).

Denmark Military Levying Rolls (2513529) is name-searchable; the Military Records wiki page and loc_001 show boys were listed from birth under their father's name from 1788/89, so the roll is direct parentage evidence. Place fields may rank rather than filter, so pair with a browse of the Thisted Amt rolls volume, which is browse-only (personCount 0), if the index underdelivers. Subject was 10 in 1789 so should appear in rolls of 1789 onward.

Parents' marriage to each other (a Niels and a wife, marriage before 1779, likely 1760s-1779). Confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's name, and its date relative to 1779 corroborates a father found indirectly. It does not alone prove Mikkel is their child. Browse marriages in the Stagstrup register (1763-1814 volume, about 3% name-indexed), widening to neighbouring parishes if absent; mother's name from any single record is not assumed to be a maiden name.

FAN/sibling item: baptisms of siblings of Mikkel naming the same Niels and mother, and baptism sponsors who are often kin, test whether the Niels in the 1779 baptism is one household. Browse the same Stagstrup register volume around the 1779 baptism.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 (1401625) is name-searchable. The 1787 and 1801 censuses place Mikkel (age about 8 and 22) in a household, possibly with Niels as head, with relationship to head in 1801. Tests the baptism and levy-roll candidate and places him in Stagstrup.

Mikkel's own marriage and burial entries (marriage entries name or imply age and parents' names; burial gives age and possibly residence), and the father's burial, which answers the objective's second part (father's death date). Sized to the father's plausible life, to about 1850 (father born c.1720-1760). Browse register volumes beyond the 1763-1814 one as listed in Denmark, Church Books.

Estate of the father Niels (death c.1780-1850, creator's lifespan sets the window) names heirs including Mikkel. Denmark Probate Indexes (2015318) are name-searchable to 1851; the Hassing Herred skifteprotokoller volume is browse-only (personCount 0). Herred assumed from the parish and must be confirmed, since the parish may lie in another herred.

- **pli_005:** Census, Muhlenberg County, 1870–1880, FamilySearch. Brackets the death window, confirms identity, and gives household members.
- **pli_006:** Cemetery and church burial records, Muhlenberg County, 1870–1911. A stone gives a date and burial place.
- **pli_007:** Newspapers, Muhlenberg County, 1870–1911, a fallback for pli_004. Looks for an obituary or estate notice.

The plan first checks for any matches already attached to his profile and quickly tests the certificate possibility. It then turns to county death registers and probate records — wills, administrator bonds, estate settlements — which are the best evidence for a pre-1911 death. The 1880 census, cemetery records, and newspaper notices are used to narrow the date and confirm identity.

1. pli_004: census, 1860, FamilySearch. Completed.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, sourced to Pennsylvania Death Certificates. loc_001 notes statewide registration began 1906, so a 1908 death has a state certificate that names father, mother (often maiden name), birthplace and informant. Read the certificate image itself rather than relying on the tree's citation. Parents named by an informant are derivative evidence.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Search for a Patrick Flynn baptism with variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Lynn. Starting-point conflict: tree fact F1 says born ~1845 in Ireland while the objective says Pennsylvania, so the baptism may be in Ireland or may not exist; Catholic registers are held by parish/diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001). A hit naming parents would be direct evidence.

The baptism may not exist (Ireland-born per F1, and Pennsylvania civil birth registration starts 1906 per loc_001), so plan Patrick's own burial entry and cemetery record after his 1908-03-12 death. Searches the name-searchable Schuylkill church collection plus cemetery/Find a Grave; burial entries may give age, birthplace or family.

The tree cites the 1850 and 1860 censuses for the Thomas Flynn parent link (R1), but Thomas is an unverified assumption (Standard 11): the 1850 census predates relationship columns and the 1860 one has none. Re-read the 1860 household and add 1880 (first with relationship to head) to test who lived with Patrick and where; the 1850 search was done under q_002. Also 1870 for Patrick's own household.

Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate parents to each other (Thomas Flynn, b. ~1818 per tree, and a wife whose name is unknown). It would confirm them as a couple and may supply the mother's name, and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas, but it does not alone prove Patrick is their child. A surname on a marriage record may be a prior married name, so also look for earlier marriages of the wife. The marriage may have been in Ireland.

Patrick's own marriage record and baptisms of his children (name-searchable church collection). Marriage entries often state age, birthplace or parents; FAN-directed: sponsors/witnesses and godparents are often kin and may name his parents or siblings.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill Register of Wills volumes image by image. Window set by the candidate parent Thomas's plausible lifespan (b. ~1818, death possible to ~1905), not Patrick's. A will or administration naming Patrick as heir would be direct parentage evidence; also check Patrick's own estate (d. 1908) for heirs and siblings.

Naturalization records for Patrick and Thomas Flynn, since F1 says Ireland-born. loc_001 flags coal-region naturalization films as often browse-only; browse as needed. Declarations state origin and arrival date, and associates serving as witnesses are FAN leads. Also plan an unscoped full-text co-occurrence search on Flynn plus the candidate mother's name once known, via full-text search.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZKR-TH2 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

The FamilySearch tree (not the project tree) records Thomas christened 14 Mar 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville, citing a Pennsylvania Catholic Church Records entry, and links him to Patrick Kerrigan (b. abt 1815, County Mayo, d. 1880 Pottsville) and Mary Gallagher (b. abt 1818, Ireland). These are leads, not proof: read the baptism entry itself for parents' names and sponsors. The Schuylkill County church collection is name-searchable; registers are held by the parish and Philadelphia diocese (loc_001), so use name variants Kerrigan/Kerrican/Kerigan/Kerrihan and Gallagher/Gallaher.

The FamilySearch tree cites the 1850 census, Pottsville, for Thomas; read the household to see whether Thomas (about 8) lives with Patrick and Mary. The 1850 census gives no relationships, so it shows co-residence only; it does not by itself prove parentage. Note siblings and neighbors.

entry.jurisdiction: Pennsylvania and Mayo, Ireland (parents' marriage, abt 1835-1841)
entry.rationale: Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate parents, Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher, to each other: confirms them as a couple, may supply Mary's maiden name (verify it is her first marriage), and its date relative to Thomas's 1842 birth corroborates the link. It does not alone prove Thomas is their child; the baptism and census place him with them. Civil marriage collections are mostly after 1677 compiled/1885+ county, so lean on the church collection and Compiled Marriages (name-searchable); a marriage may lie in Ireland if they married before emigrating.

Track Patrick, Mary and Thomas across 1860, 1870 and 1880. The 1880 schedule records relationship to head, so a Patrick Kerrigan household in 1880 (Patrick d. 1880 per FamilySearch tree) or Thomas's own household may show son/mother links; also shows siblings and neighbors (FAN). Use spelling variants.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

If the death year proves wrong, widen again (the reference is unverified).

Thomas Flynn's own burial entry. Tree S5 cites St. Mary's Catholic Church (Pottsville) baptismal registers for siblings Mary and James. loc_001: Catholic registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county, under the Diocese of Philadelphia. Burial entries often state age, origin and spouse; this also tests the 1865 death date.

If Thomas died about 1865, the 1870 census should show Patrick (about 25) and a possible widow or siblings in separate or shared households, naming the mother and her birthplace. 1860 (done) shows Patrick age 15 with Thomas; the tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland about 1845 whereas the question says Pennsylvania, so birthplace entries are also checked.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) to Patrick's mother: confirms the couple as a unit, may supply her maiden name (only if this was her first marriage; do not treat any surname as her birth name until checked), and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates the father named on the 1908 death certificate. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. The tree places the births in Ireland, so the marriage may be there; search Pennsylvania church marriage registers and note any Irish parish lead.

A death about 1865 raises the possibility of Civil War service for Thomas (about 47) or sons. Pension files for a widow or minor children name family members and are created decades after the death, so the window runs past 1870. Tests the 1865 date and could name the widow.

FAN item: siblings Mary and James Flynn (tree, from S5). Their marriage, baptism and death entries and those of their children may name Thomas and the mother, including her maiden name. A baptism for Patrick may not exist if he was born in Ireland about 1845, so his burial in 1908 is covered in the next item.

Patrick's own burial or cemetery record (death certificate found, log_005, informant son-in-law James Brown). Nearby family plots may hold Thomas, the mother and siblings, with dates that test the 1865 death. Baptism may be out of reach if the birth was in Ireland.
